translations.text: Truly, the congregation of holy people is the kingdom of heaven, because their hearts are not caught up in earthly desires; instead they yearn for the things above. God already reigns in them now, as in heavenly dwellings.

When they would not come to the wedding, he sent again, saying: "Tell those who are invited: Behold, I have prepared my good things. I have slaughtered my bulls and my fattened birds, and I have made everything ready. Come to the wedding."
The fattened birds signify the holy teachers of the New Testament.
They are so greatly fattened with the grace of the Holy Spirit that they long for the journey upward on the wings of a spiritual way of life.
And it also seems very burdensome to them that they should make their habits conform to his rule.
He destroyed the murderers, because he cruelly killed the wicked persecutors, as we read everywhere in the passions of the martyrs.
The gospel says that he burned up their city, because they will be burned in eternal torment, both in soul and in body.
"He sent his army," because he destroys the wicked through his angels. What are the hosts of angels but the army of the Heavenly King?
The king then said to his servants, "This wedding is ready, but those whom I invited to it were not worthy of it.
They gather the sinful from the righteous in bundles, when murderers are bound together in the fire of hell, thieves with thieves, the greedy with the greedy, fornicators with fornicators;
and so all wicked companions suffer together, bound up in the eternal torments; and the clean wheat is brought into God's barn.
"God loved this world so much that he gave his only-begotten Son for us." The Son of God, who came to humankind through love, indicated in the gospel what the wedding garment signified: true love.
Everyone who turns to God with faith and baptism comes to the wedding; but he does not come in a wedding garment if he does not hold to true love.
True love is this: that each person loves his friend in God and his enemy for God's sake.
And anyone he finds without true love he questions angrily, saying, "Friend, how did you dare to come to my feast without a wedding garment?"
He called him "friend", and yet he cast him out from among his guests. He was a friend through faith, and an enemy through his works.
For the prophet said to God about such people: "My Lord, your eyes have seen my imperfection, and all are written in your book."
In the outer darkness there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. There the eyes will weep in the flame of hell that now wander about, gazing, through unlawful desires;
If anyone has doubts about the resurrection, he can understand from this gospel that there will be a true resurrection, since there will be eyes and teeth there.
Eyes are made of flesh, and teeth of bone; for we must, whether we want to or not, rise at the end of this world with flesh and with bone,
and receive the reward for all our deeds: either a dwelling with God for good merits, or the torment of hell with the devil for wicked deeds.
About this the blessed Job said, "I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and I shall again be clothed with my skin,
and in my flesh I shall see God, I myself and not another." That is, not another form in my place, but I myself shall see him.
The ending of this gospel is very fearful: "Many are called, and few are chosen."
Look: the voice of all of us now calls on Christ, but the life of all of us does not call on him; for many contradict by their conduct what they profess with their voice.
Some people make a good beginning for a while, but they end in evil. Some make an evil beginning, and end well through true repentance. Some begin well, and end better.
So everyone should greatly fear for himself, even if he leads a good life, and in no way be overconfident about himself; for he does not know whether he is worthy to enter the eternal kingdom.
Nor should he despair of others, even if they fall into sins; for he does not know the manifold riches of God's mercy.
Now Saint Gregory says that a certain brother turned to a monastery that he himself had founded, and after the trial prescribed by the rule he took the monastic habit.
A brother of his by blood followed him to the monastery, not out of zeal for a good way of life, but out of fleshly affection.
The spiritual brother greatly pleased all the monks of the monastery through his good conduct, while his brother by blood strongly and perversely opposed his way of life.
He lived in the monastery out of necessity rather than to better himself. He was frivolous in speech and perverse in his deeds, well dressed in clothing and evil in his habits.
He had no patience if anyone urged him toward a good way of life. So his life became very burdensome to the brothers, but they bore it patiently for the sake of his brother's goodness.
He could not do anything good, and he would not listen to anything good. Then he was suddenly struck by a certain disease and brought to the point of death.
When he was brought to the point of departure, the brothers came to commend his soul.
He lay with his lower limbs gone cold; only in his breast did the spirit still breathe.
Then the brothers prayed for him all the more eagerly, because they saw that he would soon depart.
Then he suddenly cried out, saying, "Go away from me. Look, here a dragon has come that is to swallow me up, but he cannot because you are here.

He has seized my head in his jaws. Make room for him, so that he may torment me no longer. If I have been given to this dragon to be swallowed, why must I suffer delay because you are standing over me?"
The brothers said to him, "Why do you speak with such great despair? Mark yourself with the sign of the holy cross."
He answered as well as he could, "I would gladly bless myself with the sign of the holy cross, but I do not have the strength, because the dragon is pressing hard on me."
So the monks prostrated themselves on the ground with weeping, and began to pray more earnestly to the ruling God for his deliverance.
Then suddenly the sick young man recovered, and said in a joyful voice, "I thank God:
look, the dragon that wanted to swallow me has now been put to flight by your prayers. He has been driven away from me, and could not stand against your intercession.
Be my intercessors now, praying for my sins; for I am ready to turn to the monastic way of life and give up all worldly habits."
Then his cold limbs came back to life, and he turned to God with all his heart. Through a long illness he was set right in his conversion, and at last he died of that same illness;
but he did not see the dragon at his death, because he had overcome it by turning his heart to God.
We should not despair, even though in this present Church many are evil and few are good;
for Noah's ark on the waves of the great flood was a symbol of this Church, and it was wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.
On the lowest deck lived the fierce beasts and creeping serpents. On the second floor lived birds and clean animals.
On the third floor lived Noah with his wife, and his three sons with their three wives.
At the bottom, where the fierce beasts lived, the ark was roomy, and higher up, where the people lived, it was narrowed;
for the holy Church is very broad in carnal people and narrow in spiritual ones.
She spreads out her bosom where the fierce live in beastly ways, and she is narrowed at the end where the rational live, conducting themselves in spiritual ways;
for the holier they are in this present Church, the fewer of them there are.

There are far more people who live by their own desires than there are who set the conduct of their lives right according to God's commandments. Nevertheless, the number of holy people is always increased through the decrease of wicked people.

The number of God's chosen is not small. As Christ said in another place, "Many will come from the east and from the west, and will sit with the patriarch Abraham, and with Isaac and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven."
Again, the psalmist said of God's chosen ones, "I counted them, and their number is greater than the sand."

In this present life the chosen seem few compared with the number of the rejected. But when they are gathered into eternal life, their number will be so great that, as the prophet said, it will be more than the grains of sand.
Lead us, Almighty God, to the number of your chosen saints, into the eternal bliss of your kingdom,
which you have prepared from the beginning of the world for those who love you, you who live and reign with the Eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
